KEY MESSAGE 1...

15Z upper air analysis depicts a progressive troughing pattern 
across the eastern half of North America, featuring a longwave 
trough pivoting into Ontario and a shortwave trough ejecting into 
the TN River Valley. The latter feature is beginning to become 
absorbed into the longer-wave trough to the north, with a wide 
baroclinic leaf evident on water-vapor imagery that was advecting 
over the OH River Valley and into the CWA. Observations outside of 
WFO RLX confirm that the leading band of moist, isentropic ascent in 
the mid-levels has arrived via the presence of altostratus and 
ACCAS; and gradual destabilization of the airmass will continue to 
occur given the presence of the high-level cirrus deck. Meanwhile, 
elevated clusters of showers and thunderstorms were ongoing across 
southeastern OH, and may clip the northwestern counties. The 12Z 
objectively analyzed UA charts indicated a sharply cyclonic 
component to the southern-stream trough at 250 mb, with a belt of 
southwesterly flow between 30-40 kt within the 300-200 mb layer 
before weakening near 500 mb where broader concavity to the trough 
exists. High humidity was also observed within the high-level theta 
surfaces, amidst a very tall and skinny EML (i.e., RAOBs from nearby 
WFOs observed the top of the EML as high as 175 mb) in congruence 
with the vigorous, moist ascent. The shortwave trough is also now 
completely open compared to yesterday, with the remnant vorticity 
lobe rotating over central TN. This feature will eject northeastward 
over the CWA throughout the next 12 hours before quickly exiting to 
the northeast as its absorption into the aforementioned longwave 
trough over east-central Canada is completed.

At the surface, the warm front is now crossing north of the I-64 
corridor, and it will continue to increase in forward speed as it 
advects northeastward across the CWA. The closest cyclone is either 
on the lee of the Appalachian Mountains or in the Upper Midwest, 
thereby leaving the CWA within a broad, open moist sector as the 
warm front lifts northeastward, with dewpoints hovering in the lower 
70s area-wide. Strong heating is also underway, although the fairly 
opaque cirrus shield has prevented full insolation from occurring, 
and temperatures are expected to peak in the middle 80s. Low-level 
convergence of the higher theta-e air may spawn a surface low 
beneath the intensifying belt of divergence aloft and serve as a 
foci for organized bands of torrential rainfall. Mean wind vectors 
throughout the cloud-bearing layer are also oriented out of the 
southwest at about 20 kt per the 12Z RAOBs from WFOs ILN and RNK, 
which is parallel to the steering flow, and will pose a risk for 
cellular training.

Anomalously high PWAT values approaching 2.00", combined with MLCAPE 
values between 1,500-2,000 J/kg and cloud-layer shear magnitudes of 
25-30 kt, in conjunction with the parallel convective movement 
relative to the mean wind, has resulted in high confidence for 
multiple episodes of flash flooding this afternoon and tonight 
across the CWA. Instantaneous rain rates may exceed 2"/hr with the 
strongest storms. The Flood Watch remains in effect for all counties 
except Pocahontas County until 1 AM EDT tonight. In addition to the 
flash flooding risk, locally strong-to-severe-caliber wind gusts 
cannot be ruled out with the best-organized storms, but the threat 
this afternoon and tonight is geared towards flash flooding. Storms 
will wane from west-to-east late tonight, followed by widespread fog 
and low-level stratus during the predawn hours Sunday.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

The base of the longwave trough over east-central Canada will dig 
into the Great Lakes region Sunday, with the respective synoptic 
cold front currently located in the Upper Midwest expected to move 
into the CWA late Sunday afternoon. Prior to the arrival of the 
front, thick, low-level stratus and fog will be intact area-wide 
during the morning hours. Mixing of the airmass will be gradual, 
with most of the fog and/or low stratus dissipating by the latter 
half of the morning. Highs will breach into the middle 80s once 
again Sunday, with the airmass remaining capped near 700 mb and 
suppress any bubbling of boundary-layer cu. The most substantial 
large-scale forcing for ascent will be displaced well to the north 
of the CWA; however, frontogenetical forcing along the weakening 
cold front may result in broken line of showers and storms late 
Sunday evening into early Monday morning. Diabatic stabilization 
will result in a gradual cessation of lightning, but brief downpours 
may still accompany showers overnight Sunday into Monday, with a 
much lower risk for flash flooding, if any. Intrusion of a 1026 mb 
surface anticyclone will result in a milder day Monday before 
temperatures heat up mid-week as a subtropical ridge rotates
